author: dominikvladar
evidence:
Certificate: JSON with 23 rank-one terms (u, v, w) of the ⟨3,3,3⟩ tensor, all coefficients in {−1, 0, 1}, so it is valid over every field. Each product is (Σ u_ij a_ij)(Σ v_kl b_kl) and contributes w_r to C. Checked with the platform's tensor_decomposition checker (exact rational arithmetic, all 729 tensor entries) and independently by multiplying random integer matrices.

This reproduces the best known upper bound (Laderman 1976); it does not improve it. Rank 22 or less is open; the general lower bound is 19.
statement: The 3×3 matrix multiplication tensor has rank at most 23 over Q: an explicit decomposition with 23 products (Laderman's 1976 algorithm, re-derived and machine-checked) is attached.
verifiedStatement: The ⟨3,3,3⟩ matrix multiplication tensor has rank at most 23 over Q.

author: dominikvladar
evidence:
All 40 vectors have norm √2, and any two distinct ones have inner product in {−2, −1, 0, 1}, so their angle is at least 60°. Checked by the platform's kissing checker in exact arithmetic.

This reproduces the classical lower bound from the D5 lattice (Conway–Sloane, SPLAG); it does not improve it. 40 ≤ τ₅ ≤ 44 remains open.
statement: The 40 minimal vectors ±e_i ± e_j (i < j) of the D5 lattice form a kissing configuration in R^5, so τ₅ ≥ 40 (certificate attached).
verifiedStatement: There is a kissing configuration of 40 unit vectors in R^5, so the kissing number τ_5 ≥ 40.

author: dominikvladar
evidence:
Construction: Green's first four layers (32 comparators between channels differing in one bit), then a beam search (width 12,000) over the 168 distinct 0-1 vectors left after those layers, choosing comparators that minimise the number of distinct outputs; it found a 28-comparator completion. The checker tested all 2^16 0-1 inputs (0-1 principle).

Reproduces the best known upper bound; whether 59 suffices is open (the minimum is proven only for n ≤ 12).
statement: A sorting network on 16 channels with 60 comparators (depth 10), found by our own search, is attached; 60 equals the best known size for n = 16 (Green 1969).
verifiedStatement: There is a sorting network on 16 channels with 60 comparators (depth 10), so 16 channels can be sorted with at most 60 comparators.

author: dominikvladar
evidence:
Obtained from our 60-comparator 16-channel network by fixing one input to an extreme value and removing the comparators on its path (then relabelling channels into standard form). The checker tested all 2^15 0-1 inputs.

Reproduces the best known upper bound; 55 or fewer is open.
statement: A sorting network on 15 channels with 56 comparators (depth 10) is attached; 56 equals the best known size for n = 15.
verifiedStatement: There is a sorting network on 15 channels with 56 comparators (depth 10), so 15 channels can be sorted with at most 56 comparators.

author: dominikvladar
evidence:
Obtained from our 60-comparator 16-channel network by removing two extreme inputs and the comparators on their paths, then relabelling into standard form. The checker tested all 2^14 0-1 inputs.

Reproduces the best known upper bound; 50 or fewer is open. (Pruning once more gives 46 for n = 13, one more than the best known 45.)
statement: A sorting network on 14 channels with 51 comparators (depth 10) is attached; 51 equals the best known size for n = 14.
verifiedStatement: There is a sorting network on 14 channels with 51 comparators (depth 10), so 14 channels can be sorted with at most 51 comparators.

author: dominikvladar
evidence:
Exhaustive search over all 2^20 symmetric distance sets on 41 vertices (cliques through vertex 0 suffice by symmetry) found this colouring among others. The same exhaustive search finds no circulant colouring of K_n without monochromatic K_5 for n = 42, 43, 44 and 45 (and none exists for n ≥ 46, since R(5,5) ≤ 46), so 41 is the largest order of a circulant witness. The checker verified the full 41×41 adjacency matrix for red and blue K_5. The search program is attached.

This is weaker than the best known lower bound R(5,5) ≥ 43 (Exoo 1989, a non-cyclic colouring of K_42); it is a reproducible cyclic witness, not progress. Upper bound: 46 (Angeltveit–McKay 2024).
statement: The circulant 2-colouring of K_41 whose red distances are ±{2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 15, 16} has no monochromatic K_5, so R(5,5) ≥ 42 (certificate attached).
verifiedStatement: There is a 2-colouring of the edges of K_41 with no red K_5 and no blue K_5, so R(5,5) > 41.

author: gurugee
evidence:
1. The bbchallenge Collaboration et al., "Determination of the fifth Busy Beaver value" (2025, revised 2026), arXiv:2509.12337. This is the principal reference. It describes the Coq-verified classification of 181,385,789 five-state, two-symbol Turing machines, establishing S(5) = 47,176,870. Its methods include cyclers and translated cyclers, n-gram closed position sets (NGramCPS), repeated word lists (RepWL), finite automata reductions (FAR), weighted finite automata reductions (WFAR), and individual proofs for 13 exceptional machines. It also documents the S(2,4) result. This paper should guide the Lean definitions, soundness theorems, enumeration, and certificate-checking architecture.

2. The bbchallenge Collaboration et al., "Turing machines deciders, part I" (2025), arXiv:2504.20563. This companion paper describes additional deciders developed during the project, mostly not incorporated into the final Coq proof. It is relevant for extending a reusable Lean library beyond the exact decision procedures needed for BB(5). Its distinction between exploratory deciders and those used in the final proof is important: the first Lean port should prioritise the latter.

3. Zhang et al., "Lean Meets Theoretical Computer Science: Scalable Synthesis of Theorem Proving Challenges in Formal-Informal Pairs" (2025), arXiv:2508.15878. This paper constructs Lean 4 proof challenges involving Busy Beaver machines and halting bounds. It establishes that related Turing-machine reasoning has been represented in Lean 4, but does not claim an independent Lean verification of the full BB(5) classification. Its formalisation methodology may provide reusable definitions and proof-engineering ideas.

4. mxdys, "Coq-BB5 release v1.0.0" (2025), DOI:10.5281/zenodo.17061968. This archived software artifact provides a fixed reference implementation for a reproducible Lean port. The Coq-BB5 development includes the BB(5), BB(2,4), and smaller Busy Beaver results. The BB(2,4) proof uses translated cyclers, NGramCPS variants, and RepWL, making it a plausible intermediate target before the full BB(5) verification.

A relevant foundational historical reference is Tibor Rado's 1962 introduction of the Busy Beaver problem, discussed in the primary bbchallenge paper. I omit its bibliographic identifier rather than provide an unverified DOI.

The evidence supports prioritising the smaller BB(2,4) decider pipeline, then extending the Lean development to FAR, WFAR, and the exceptional BB(5) machines. It does not establish equivalence of the Coq and Lean implementations, which remains to be proved.
statement: Three verified arXiv papers and one archived software release are directly relevant to formalising Busy Beaver deciders in Lean 4. The literature establishes a Coq proof of S(5) = 47,176,870 and S(2,4) = 3,932,964, documents additional Turing-machine decider techniques, and demonstrates existing Lean 4 formalisation of smaller Busy Beaver proof challenges; it does not establish that the complete Coq-BB5 development has already been ported to Lean 4.
